turn_text: Yeah, I know I followed you quite extensively because you did so much in the energy field while you were a senator. You know, of course, your ideas on different issues evolve, but I've always thought that compromise in our political discourse and work was important, listening to the other side. thinking that no particular party was going to be right on every subject every day, every proposal and being open to listen to Republicans working with them, particularly when I felt like it was the best thing for the country or for my state. So I've been sort of long in that central spot, followed the work of Bill Clinton and Al Gore and folks like Joe Lieberman and John McCain. The art of compromise, the art of being able to work with the other side, it's become very, very polarizing and very unfortunate. And I think detrimental to our country. Part of it is because of the gerrymandering that has occurred in both parties or guilty of it, but creating districts, let's say, for the House of Representatives that are either hardcore Republican or hardcore Democrats. So that's one problem that's been identified, no easy solutions for it. It's because more people are producing gas. We want to lift that band. That's one policy change. So if President Trump is reelected or President Biden is reelected, I'm working with a group of members, House and Senate, to try to get that band lifted. I think building more natural gas pipelines is important. And there are environmental restrictions that were not fashioned to be weapons against pipelines, as you know, but they have become such The country operates under the Natural Gas Act, which basically says that FERC, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, if they believe a pipeline is in the public interest, they have to look at all the different factors and they make the decision. And if they agree that pipelines should go in, the pipeline should be built. Well, what's happening is some counties and some states, blue counties, blue states, more liberal leaning, are using the Clean Water Act to basically veto a pipeline. That would be like giving a community veto power over a interstate. So like you build a whole interstate from Florida, and you're almost to California, and then some state says, oh, I'm sorry, you can't build this, you know, these last five miles. Well, how could you ever connect the country? Local governments have rights, of course, to cite certain things. They have rights to talk about whether they think this is in their interest or not, but they should not have, in my view of many, just blanket veto power because, oh, we don't like pipelines. And so we've got to get more pipelines built, not just for natural gas, but also for removing carbon CO2. So we need CO2 pipelines. We need more hydrogen pipelines. turn_text: And you mention how expensive gas is in Europe, and much of that is because Europeans had relied very heavily on Russian natural gas, as you mentioned, and with the invasion into the Ukraine, people have cut back or even completely eliminated Russian gas from the mix. They shut down their own coal production and domestic gas production in Norway. They put all sorts of tough restrictions, you know, Norway has that North Sea and that robust offshore drilling, which they still do. Europe needs to produce more energy, not less, and they're not doing that. They're shutting down, and their prices are going up. And then they want to yell at us because they have to pay a lot on the spot market. Inflation is high in Europe. People are very, very upset. They're losing their manufacturing base to us. And I want to do everything I can to not have America follow that path. We need our own path. I don't know what Europe's going to do, but that's what we're trying to get done here. That's what Natural Allies is preaching. I have another group that I helped to organize with Carlos Cabello with the Climate Solutions Caucus. And I'm so proud of this because we have 64 members of the House and 12 members of the Senate.
